title: India Is Paying Russia a 425% Higher Premium for Oil. It Is Buying More Anyway.
excerpt: Russia's share of India's crude imports jumped to an 11-month high of 38 per cent in April as the West Asia crisis forced New Delhi to scramble for every barrel it could find
body:
The discount is gone. The volumes are up. And India is paying for it.

Russia's share in the value of India's oil imports surged to an 11-month high of 37.7 per cent in April 2026, according to trade data released this week. India paid an average of $864.9 per tonne for Russian crude — well above the $787.1 per tonne average it paid across all suppliers. The premium of $77.8 per tonne represents a staggering 425 per cent increase from March, when India was paying just $14.8 per tonne above the global average for Russian barrels.

The shift encapsulates the new reality of India's energy economy: the cheap Russian oil that powered India's post-2022 energy strategy is no longer cheap. But India is buying more of it anyway.

## How We Got Here

The story begins in February 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine triggered Western sanctions on Russian crude. India, which had imported less than 2 per cent of its oil from Russia before the war, saw an opportunity. As European buyers turned away, Indian refiners swooped in, purchasing Russian crude at steep discounts — sometimes $20 to $30 below Brent. By mid-2025, Russia was supplying nearly 2 million barrels per day to India, making it the country's single largest crude supplier.

Then the West Asia crisis changed the calculus. When US-Israeli strikes against Iran began in late February 2026 and the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, roughly 20 per cent of global oil supply was impaired. Middle Eastern barrels that India had traditionally relied on — from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Kuwait — became harder and more expensive to source.

India pivoted back to Russia. But this time, the leverage had shifted.

## The Premium Problem

In the pre-Hormuz world, India bought Russian crude because it was the cheapest option. Russian oil was typically 7 to 13 per cent cheaper than equivalent grades from Saudi Arabia or the UAE. That arithmetic was the entire justification for New Delhi's diplomatic gymnastics — maintaining the Russia relationship while absorbing Western criticism.

Now, with global supply constrained and every major importer scrambling for non-Hormuz barrels, Russia is no longer offering discounts. It is commanding premiums. India paid Russia $864.9 per tonne in April, while the overall average across all suppliers was $787.1 — meaning Russian crude was nearly 10 per cent more expensive than the blend.

The premium surge — from $14.8 per tonne in March to $77.8 in April — reflects the speed at which the physical oil market has tightened. Traders report that Russian crude is now being priced against Brent with minimal or no discount, a far cry from the $20-off era of 2023.

## The Import Bill Is Ballooning

India's total oil imports in April hit 195.3 lakh tonnes, a 23 per cent increase year-on-year. The import bill ballooned to $15.4 billion, up 61.3 per cent from the same month last year. The widening gap between volume growth (23 per cent) and value growth (61 per cent) tells the cost story at a glance: India is importing somewhat more oil, but paying far more per barrel.

Meanwhile, the US share of India's oil imports fell to an eight-month low of 2.9 per cent in April. The decline is significant given that Washington had been pushing New Delhi to increase American crude purchases as part of the interim trade deal framework. The numbers suggest that Indian refiners are prioritising availability over diplomatic optics.

## What India Is Actually Doing

Behind the headline numbers, India's energy bureaucracy is working multiple tracks simultaneously. State refiners — Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum, Hindustan Petroleum, and Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals — have collectively purchased roughly 20 million barrels of Russian oil from traders in recent weeks, according to Reuters.

New Delhi has reportedly approached the Trump administration seeking explicit approval to increase Russian crude purchases specifically because of the Iran conflict — a diplomatic reversal from the first quarter of 2026, when India was curtailing Russian imports under US pressure.

The Kremlin has noticed. "The war in Iran has fuelled demand for Russian energy products," spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Friday, noting that buyers like India and China were "guided by their national interests."

## The NRI Angle

For the Indian diaspora, the oil import story has direct downstream consequences. A ballooning energy import bill puts pressure on the rupee, drives up imported inflation and constrains the fiscal space available for subsidies and social spending. The commercial LPG cylinder price was hiked by ₹42 in Delhi effective June 1, while petrol and diesel pump prices remain frozen only because the government is absorbing the difference through reduced excise collections.

India imports over 85 per cent of its crude oil. With strategic reserves covering only about 25 days of demand and global inventories at critically low levels, the country's energy security equation remains precarious. The return to premium-priced Russian crude is not a strategy — it is a stopgap. The question is how long the stopgap needs to last.
